title: Fire-Line Readiness Passport for Contract Wildfire Crews
one_liner: A qualifications, equipment-inspection and shift-ticket system for private wildland fire engine and crew owners, built so they are never rejected at check-in or paid late.
customer: Owners of private wildland fire engines, hand crews and water tenders contracted by federal and state agencies (the national association alone represents 300+ contractors). A single rig or crew can gross six figures in a season.
problem: Contract fire resources are dispatched from agency lists and must show current qualifications, red cards, fitness tests, insurance, vehicle and pump inspections and correct rate documentation. A missing or expired item gets the rig rejected or sent home at check-in. Payment then depends on shift tickets being filled out and reconciled correctly. Errors mean holds and weeks of waiting while the owner fronts payroll, fuel and insurance. Most operators run this on paper and text messages.
solution: A mobile passport per crew member and rig. It tracks qualification and training expiry, physical and medical dates, insurance certificates and equipment checklists against the specific contract's rules. It flags what will fail at check-in, generates GPS-and-time-stamped shift tickets in agency format with automated checks against contract rates, and packages payment documents. Later it adds accelerated payment.
why_now: Agencies are leaning heavily on contractors, the national Type 2-IA crew contract cycle continues through 2026-27, and the wildfire workforce and pay rules are shifting. It is late September, so the off-season sales window for 2027 contracts is open and there is time to build an MVP before next season.
revenue_model: $150-400 per engine or crew per month. A 1-2% fee on accelerated payment advances against verified, error-free packets, once the record system proves low rejection rates. Insurance and training referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In fire contracting, the paperwork is the collateral. The rig-days lost to rejection and the payment delays from ticket errors are the real costs. A system that pre-validates packets against the contract's own rules is trusted by agencies, insurers and factoring companies alike, so it can become the data layer for everything financial in the niche. The market looks small (roughly a thousand firms), but each firm has an unusually high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Join the national contractor association's conversations and contact owners on state preseason contract lists in Oregon, Idaho, Montana and California. Offer a $750-1,500 'pre-season readiness audit' per rig, mapping each contract's checklist. Use the audits to design the MVP. Sell subscriptions from February for the 2027 season.

title: Beneficiary-Funded Dynamic Line Ratings
one_liner: Skip the utility's missing incentive: let the data center or generator that needs capacity pay for dynamic line ratings and take a slice of the capacity released.
customer: Data center developers and congestion-constrained renewable, storage and merchant generation owners. The utility is a passive partner.
problem: Dynamic line rating adds 30-50% capacity at about a tenth of the cost of reconductoring, but utilities earn no return on operating savings, so adoption is stuck. Projects held back by a few constrained lines lose years or revenue.
solution: A special-purpose company funds and deploys DLR (sensors plus weather-model virtual ratings) on the specific lines limiting a beneficiary's project. A three-party agreement has the utility accept ratings with a safety margin and keep the reliability data, the beneficiary gets earlier energization or less curtailment, and the company earns a capacity-uplift fee for about 10 years.
why_now: Automated study tools (Tapestry ran ~220 GW of PJM applications in under an hour) show speed is possible. FERC's ambient-adjusted ratings rule and GETs consideration laws mainstream the concept. Cost of delay is enormous.
revenue_model: Cost-plus up-front sensors and analytics, plus an annual $/kW capacity-uplift fee or a share of avoided curtailment.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders wait for the utility's incentive to change, and it will not. Contract the incentive from the customer instead. That is structurally a customer-funded upgrade, which utilities already know how to accept.
first_30_days: Use public congestion and rating data to find the 20 lines most limiting renewables and large loads. Sell three $25-60k congestion and rating audits to constrained project owners. Recruit one utility engineering champion. Resell sensors from an existing DLR vendor.

title: Contingency Refunds for Fake Local-Service Leads
one_liner: A win-based service that audits what plumbers, HVAC firms, locksmiths, law offices and clinics pay per lead or call, proves which were bots, spam or out-of-area, and files the platform disputes owners never get around to.
customer: Owner-operators of 1-20 person home-service, legal and clinic businesses spending $1.5K-15K/month on Google Local Services Ads, Thumbtack, Angi, Yelp and tracked call numbers. Fee is 25% of credits recovered.
problem: 'Reaching customers' is the number-one small-business challenge (Fed SBCS 2026) while legacy local-marketing vendors shrink (Thryv 2025 revenue $785M, down). Owners pay per lead but cannot tell real jobs from junk, and platform dispute windows are short and evidence-heavy, so credits likely go unclaimed (my inference; recovery rates need testing). Bot share of web traffic is estimated anywhere from about 20% (Cloudflare CEO) to over 50% (Imperva/Fortune), and cheap AI voice agents make robo-calls to paid numbers easier.
solution: The owner connects ad and lead accounts or forwards lead emails and call-tracking numbers. The system transcribes calls, scores caller numbers, checks geography and duplicates, classifies wrong-service and spam leads, and flags synthetic voices. It assembles evidence and files disputes inside each platform's window, reconciles the credits, and reports a monthly verified-lead rate per channel to guide budget.
why_now: Speech-to-text and classification now cost pennies per call. AI-generated traffic is polluting pay-per-lead channels while platform-native verification stays thin. Small owners have less time and money than ever, and outcome-priced recovery is exactly what subscription incumbents cannot easily offer.
revenue_model: 25% of credits recovered, plus a $49/month scorecard after month 3. Later add white-label to marketing agencies and sell verified-lead-rate benchmarks.
non_obvious_insight: Platforms already built refund mechanisms and profit from friction, so packaging evidence on time is the whole product. The independent verified-lead rate per channel is the first honest ROI data most SMBs ever get, and it may end up worth more than the refunds. Contingency pricing works because credits appear as visible cash in the ad account.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 owners from HVAC, garage-door, locksmith and plumber Facebook groups with a free 60-day lookback audit. Contract VAs to file disputes manually and measure recovery as a percent of spend. Publish a junk-lead-rate benchmark by platform, and build software only once recovery exceeds roughly 8% of spend.

title: Private Road Associations in a Box
one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.

title: Local-Law Radar for Data Center and Battery Developers
one_liner: A system that continuously reads city and county codes, planning agendas and minutes nationwide and warns developers which jurisdictions are drafting moratoria or new setback, noise and fire-safety rules before they pass.
customer: Land-acquisition and permitting teams at data-center, battery-storage, solar, EV-charging and peaker developers, siting consultants, and law-firm land-use groups.
problem: Local ordinances decide whether $100M-$1B projects get built, but roughly 19,000 municipalities publish codes and agendas as PDFs on inconsistent sites. Opposition-driven moratoria appear with weeks of notice, developers learn about them after buying land options, and existing zoning datasets capture setbacks and floor-area ratios, not conditional-use or moratorium rules for new infrastructure types.
solution: A scraper and LLM pipeline over municipal-code hosts and agenda platforms (Legistar, CivicClerk, PrimeGov and similar) that classifies items by project type, alerts on early signals ('first reading', 'study session', 'interim urgency ordinance'), answers 'is X permitted at parcel Y and under what conditions?', and scores county risk. Two land-use paralegals curate the output.
why_now: Data-center and battery-storage siting fights surged through 2025-26, including after the Jan 2025 Moss Landing battery fire (background, verify), and LLMs can now read messy municipal PDFs cheaply enough to cover thousands of jurisdictions.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per developer team, $60-250k/year enterprise plans, and $500-2,000 per-parcel reports.
non_obvious_insight: Moratoria are telegraphed weeks ahead in public agendas that nobody reads at scale, so the value is the leading indicator, not the code text. A stranded land option costs far more than the subscription.
first_30_days: Cover the three states with the most data-center activity and track about 500 jurisdictions' agendas. Publish a weekly free moratorium tracker, sell five developers or site-selection consultants at $2.5k/month, and back-test which past moratoria would have been flagged 30 days early.

title: Low-Background Human Data: Witnessed Creative Corpora
one_liner: Like pre-war steel, certifiably human creative work is becoming scarce, so sell fresh, witnessed, process-verified corpora to labs and detector vendors.
customer: AI labs and evaluation teams, detector vendors that need gold human test sets, and data-licensing brokers.
problem: Anything scraped from the web after 2023 is contaminated (AI is over 50% of Deezer daily uploads, and large shares of text are machine-made). Labs need uncontaminated creative data for evals, style diversity and fine-tuning. Detector vendors need known-human sets to measure false positives. No one can currently prove any given item is human.
solution: A paid panel of ID-verified writers, illustrators and musicians produce work under witnessed capture (screen and keystroke logs, DAW session logs, timelapse). Each item ships with process evidence in a quarterly dataset subscription. Creators are paid per item plus royalties from dataset revenue. Start with a 5,000-item 'human baseline' across text, illustration and music.
why_now: Contamination is now measurable, detector-scoring consequences are public, and human data has become a large market. Process-capture tooling for creative apps is cheap.
revenue_model: $25-300k per dataset subscription, per-item pricing of $5-200, and evaluation-as-a-service, with 50-60% of revenue to creators.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not more data but certifiably unpolluted data, and every improvement in AI raises its price. The premium for 'guaranteed human' is set by buyers who cannot get it anywhere else.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 creators from paid-newsletter and Discord communities. Build a capture app (browser extension plus DAW logging). Send a sample data card to detector vendors and two labs' eval teams, and sell a $25-75k baseline set.

title: Practice-in-a-Box for Licensed Paraprofessionals
one_liner: Turn displaced paralegals into licensed legal paraprofessionals who can legally sell AI-leveraged flat-fee services directly to the public in states that now allow it.
customer: Displaced or at-risk paralegals and legal assistants, paying $149-299/month, who serve consumers with family law, landlord-tenant, and limited civil matters in states with limited-license programs (Arizona LP, Utah LPP, Oregon LP, Colorado LLP, Minnesota developing).
problem: AI has pushed the value of routine paralegal tasks toward zero inside law firms, while most low-income people's legal problems get little or no help. Several states created limited licenses for exactly this gap, but the licensed pool is tiny because the path (exams, supervised hours, malpractice insurance, trust accounting, client acquisition, tooling) is costly and lonely for a laid-off individual.
solution: A 'practice in a box' with exam and supervised-hours prep, a group malpractice policy, compliant trust accounting, standard intake and scope-check forms, an AI drafting stack with mandatory citation verification and human sign-off, and shared consumer marketing for flat-fee packages (for example, $900 uncontested divorce). It hands off cleanly to lawyers when a matter is out of scope. To respect fee-sharing rules, the company charges flat subscription fees, never a percentage of legal fees.
why_now: Entry-level paralegal roles are among the most cited casualties of 2026 AI layoffs. Colorado's LLP program launched in 2024, Arizona's has licensed since 2021, and Oregon approved its license in 2022. AI drafting makes flat-fee economics finally work for a solo practitioner.
revenue_model: $149-299/month practitioner subscription, exam-prep courses (about $600), group insurance commissions, and per-practitioner advertising placements where permitted.
non_obvious_insight: When AI drives the cost of doing legal work to near zero, the scarce asset is the license to sell it. Regulators created cheap licenses for access-to-justice reasons and they sit underused. Displaced paralegals are the natural supply. The moat is regulatory and operational, not technological.
first_30_days: Pick Arizona and Colorado. Recruit 15 laid-off paralegals through paralegal associations and LinkedIn. Sign a malpractice broker. Launch a $49 'is my matter in scope?' consumer screen as lead generation. Sell exam-prep and onboarding to the first 10 practitioners, about $2k in monthly recurring revenue plus course fees.

title: Recurring-Route Repricing Desk for Service Owners
one_liner: Read-only connect a lawn, pool, cleaning or pest route to its books, find the customers who are losing money, and hand the owner ready-to-send price-increase letters.
customer: Owners of 2-15 person recurring-service companies (lawn, pool, cleaning, pest, window) on Jobber, Housecall Pro or ServiceM8 plus QuickBooks. They pay a one-time audit fee, then a monthly retainer.
problem: Owners discover their margin problem after the fact. r/sweatystartup: "Profitable jobs on paper keep turning into break-even or worse when I look at the actual numbers after" (82/100). A Jobber Community thread is titled "Anyone else realize they were breaking even or losing money after expenses?", and its owner had a full schedule but jobs barely broke even once true payroll burden (taxes, workers comp), supplies, insurance and transaction fees were counted. Tools do not fix it: Jobber adds job costing only on its $39-199/mo plans, and Joist stops at $8/mo estimates. Fear of losing the client keeps owners from raising prices.
solution: 1) A read-only connection or CSV export of Jobber or Housecall Pro, QuickBooks or Stripe, and payroll. 2) Per-customer true margin, including labor burden, drive time, card fees and callbacks. 3) A ranked list of customers to raise by X%, re-scope or drop. 4) Auto-drafted price-increase notices, phone scripts and rebuttals for the "I'll go elsewhere" reply. 5) A churn tracker that shows what each increase cost or earned. It is sold as a productized service backed by software, not as a dashboard.
why_now: Owners are absorbing cost increases in labor, insurance and materials and cannot afford to keep pricing by feel. LLMs let a two-person team parse messy exports and receipts and allocate costs per customer, which used to take a bookkeeper hours. Incumbent field-service tools keep gating job costing behind upper tiers.
revenue_model: $149 one-time margin audit. $99-199/mo retainer for monthly re-scoring, letters and churn tracking. Optional 10% referral to insurers or payroll partners.
non_obvious_insight: Every field-service tool records revenue. The missing piece is cost allocation and the nerve to raise prices, so the paid deliverable is the letter and the script, not another dashboard. Evidence: r/sweatystartup cluster "Unprofitable Service Jobs" and "How do you price your cleaning jobs? Looking to update my rates" (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/sweatystartup). The owner-facing forum thread is at https://community.getjobber.com/discussions/finances-forum/anyone-else-realize-they-were-breaking-even-or-losing-money-after-expenses/9694. Job costing is gated to $39-199/mo tiers and estimate tools stop at $8/mo (https://www.microgaps.com/blog/saas-niches-nobody-talking-about-2026). r/smallbusiness shows the fear: "Should I fire a client that's 50% of my revenue?" and "Client sent me a 1-star review because I charged for extra work" (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/smallbusiness). SaaS is structurally a poor fit for tiny businesses, so a service with custom tooling wins here (https://beekeycheung.substack.com/p/saas-products-leave-small-businesses).
first_30_days: Week 1: post in r/sweatystartup and the Jobber Community offering 10 free margin audits from a CSV export. Weeks 2-3: do them by hand in a spreadsheet and record which customers each owner would raise or drop. Week 4: convert to $149 audits and pre-sell the $99/mo retainer to the first 5. Target 20 paid audits and 5 retainers within the first two months.

title: Sole-source price-reasonableness memos from council agenda data
one_liner: A buy-side benchmark built from public council packets showing what other governments pay Tyler, Axon, OpenGov and Flock, sold as the missing price-reasonableness memo for every sole-source renewal.
customer: Finance directors, IT directors, purchasing officers and clerks in cities and counties of 5k-250k renewing proprietary software (ERP, permitting, body cameras, ALPR). They pay $495-$1,500 per renewal brief or $3k/year subscription. Councilmembers who want a sanity check are the second audience.
problem: Vendors keep pricing confidential, and sole-source renewals sail through with no comparison. Steuben County, NY approved a five-year Tyler MUNIS/Enterprise renewal at $287,644 in 2026/27 rising 5% a year to $349,633, and the record shows no benchmarking or alternatives (5-0 vote, July 14, 2026). Danbury, CT renewed OpenGov ($71,490.65) and Tyler MUNIS ($299,274.89) unanimously as sole-source because each vendor 'is the developer of proprietary systems' (Aug 5, 2026). In National City, CA a councilmember balked at a $250,000 Tyler budgeting module ('It is a $250,000'), the public questioned the sole-source, and the council demanded a white paper with precise terms and fees.
solution: Continuously ingest agenda packets from the big agenda platforms (Legistar, Granicus, CivicClerk, CivicPlus AgendaCenter) and use LLM extraction to build a structured contract table: vendor, product, price, term, escalator, termination clause, and normalized unit metrics (per capita, per seat, per officer, per camera). Anyone facing a renewal enters the vendor and product and gets a one-page brief within a day. It gives the comparable set, the median escalator, the clauses other governments got (price caps, termination for convenience, data-export rights) and a draft sole-source price-reasonableness paragraph the purchasing officer can attach to the staff report. Later: optional negotiation support on success fee.
why_now: Multi-year Tyler and other vendor contracts are coming up for renewal in 2026, and budgets are squeezed by federal cost shifts (SNAP admin share rising to 75% in October 2026) and grant uncertainty. Agenda packets are now machine-readable at scale. Cheap LLM extraction turns a decade of scattered PDFs into a price table, which was not economically possible before.
revenue_model: $495-1,500 per renewal brief; $3k/year unlimited briefs for a county; 15% of first-year savings for negotiated renewals. Secondary revenue: a quarterly 'what governments pay' index for councils and state associations of counties.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce item is not the data, it is a price-reasonableness determination. Sole-source is only defensible when the buyer can document that the price is reasonable, and none of these records shows one. The public packets already contain the answer, and every vendor claims pricing is confidential while its own contracts are posted in agenda PDFs. Evidence: Steuben County renewal, no alternatives documented (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9150000/new-york/steuben-county/finance-secures-fiveyear-renewal-pricing-for-munisenterprise-erp-committee-approves); Danbury sole-source renewals (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8951200/connecticut/fairfield/danbury-city/board-renews-opengov-and-tyler-munis-contracts-totaling-roughly-370000); National City council asking for the terms and fees (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9526083/california/san-diego-county/national-city/council-asks-city-manager-for-white-paper-after-tyler-technologies-budgeting-demo). Elko's five-year Axon extension at about $91,200 a year is another comparable data point (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog).
first_30_days: Scrape agenda packets from 300 mid-size jurisdictions in 2 states and extract about 500 contracts for 5 vendors. Publish a free 'What governments actually pay Tyler' leaderboard to earn inbound. Identify contracts expiring in 6-9 months from the term dates in old packets and email those finance directors a free sample brief. Sell the first 10 briefs at $495. Get 2 governments to attach the memo to a staff report as a proof point.

title: Tooling Hostage: Repatriate Molds and Dies
one_liner: Extract molds, dies and fixtures from Asian suppliers, refurbish them, and re-home them with US or nearshore shops.
customer: Consumer-product and industrial OEMs with $10M-$500M revenue and $50k-$2M of tooling sitting at Asian contract manufacturers, plus the new US or Mexican shops that will use it.
problem: Tariffs, a USMCA that was not renewed, and a war shock (freight up to 50%) push companies to move production. The first blocker is the tooling. Ownership is ambiguous, suppliers demand payoffs, drawings are missing, and nobody handles inspection, crating, freight and requalification as one service.
solution: Step 1 is a fixed-fee Tool Audit covering contract review, inspection video, location, condition and cost to escape. Step 2 is turnkey extraction: a local agent and letter, crating, freight and a customs review of the tooling's duty class. Step 3 is US refurbishment and first-article requalification through partner shops. Step 4 is a scan-and-drawing escrow so the next move is easy.
why_now: Companies are re-sourcing now under the rebuilt tariff regime. Freight and war-risk surcharges make each move costly, and the first-mover on tool logistics is unclaimed territory.
revenue_model: Audit at $2.5-5k. Extraction at $8-40k or 10-15% of tooling value. Refurbishment and requalification pass-through at about 15% margin. Escrow subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The lock-in in Asia is the tool, not cheap labor, and the tool's legal owner is often unclear. Whoever holds the tool controls the reshoring decision, so extraction is the real first step. Duty treatment of imported tooling and Chinese export or IP disputes need counsel.
first_30_days: Publish a 'Where are your tools?' checklist. Run 5 audits for hardware brands found via trade shows and Amazon brand lists. Hire a fixer and lawyer in Shenzhen or Ningbo. Line up one refurbishment partner shop in Ohio or Michigan.

title: Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors
one_liner: Sell seed VCs, pharma BD teams and AI-bio founders confidential 'does this paper's key result actually work?' intelligence, from anonymous postdoc consensus polls up to paid replication of the one key experiment.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms, pharma BD and scouting teams evaluating academic spinouts or in-licensing, and AI-bio startups building on published wet-lab claims. Pay $4-6k for a poll-only memo and $15-40k for a key-experiment replication.
problem: Investors and BD teams can't tell which high-profile papers replicate. The truth exists as hallway consensus: 'that result only works in the first author's hands', 'nobody outside that lab can get the organoid protocol to run', 'cells were cultured as previously described' with four layers of citations. Formal diligence hires KOL consultants who are conflicted and often the PI's friends, or a CRO that needs 4 months and a full protocol. Bad academic-asset bets burn $5-20M before anyone notices.
solution: Wedge product 'Bench Pulse': in 5 business days, poll 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous postdocs and senior techs working in the exact subfield about the named claim, reagents and protocol. Deliver a structured memo with consensus, red flags, the Figure-3 problem, which reagents or lots are fragile, and a 'what to test first' plan. Upsell: 'Key-Figure Replication'. A pool of laid-off or between-position scientists runs the single decisive experiment in 3-4 weeks in rented bench space (not on university property), with pre-registered success criteria and blinded readout.
why_now: Biotech funding since 2023 rewards capital efficiency, so seed funds want cheaper, faster kill decisions. Pharma is shopping for early assets in academia and abroad. AI-bio companies are building on published wet-lab claims with little bench sense. NIH disruption and biotech layoffs have released a large pool of very good bench scientists who want paid, flexible work. Expert-network compliance norms are now well understood, so a compliant structure is feasible.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee per poll memo and per replication study. Annual retainer for funds that want a pipeline-wide 'bench pulse' (about $30-60k). Optional success-fee or advisory equity for AI-bio startups.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not lab capacity, it is candid consensus. Replication is expensive, but the postdoc informal network already knows which labs' results hold up. The winning move is to monetize that gossip compliantly and only spend on replication after the poll narrows the question. GLG-style expert calls fail because they interview one conflicted senior person instead of 10 juniors who actually do the pipetting.
first_30_days: Choose one subfield you personally have 20 contacts in (for example CAR-T, organoids, targeted protein degradation or spatial biology). Build the compliant NDA plus anonymity protocol with a lawyer for about $3k. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on one asset they are already looking at. Convert the fund that reacts to a paid $5k poll, then upsell one replication. Pay panelists $150-300 per poll from the first revenue.

title: Weaver Ant Crews for Cashew and Mango Orchards
one_liner: Orchard pest control by living ant colonies: trained local 'ant agents' seed, feed and maintain weaver ants in smallholder cashew and mango trees, and the farmers get paid a residue-free premium.
customer: Smallholder cashew and mango cooperatives in Vietnam, Tanzania and West Africa, and the processors and exporters who need residue-free nuts and fruit.
problem: Smallholders spray expensive pesticides to fight coconut bugs, mirids and thrips. Costs are high, farmer health suffers, and exporters worry about residue limits. Biological control from imported predators is out of reach for smallholders.
solution: Weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina and O. longinoda) are territorial predators that guard trees against most pests. Our agents seed colonies, connect tree crowns with rope bridges, and supply sugar and protein supplements in the dry season. Cooperatives sign a per-tree, per-season contract. A phone-based check of nest counts and canopy occupancy generates a verified 'pesticide-free days' record that supports premium pricing with buyers.
why_now: Field research already supports it. In Vietnamese mixed pomelo and orange plantations, lower costs from ant treatments produced profit gains of 47% over pesticide plots. Economic studies of African weaver ants exist for Tanzanian cashew, and Vietnamese cashew smallholders (more than 200,000 households) are pesticide-dependent. What is new is cheap phone-based computer vision to verify colony presence, and buyers tightening residue limits.
revenue_model: A per-tree, per-season service fee set below current spray spend, plus a share (for example 10-15%) of any quality or premium uplift negotiated with exporters. Buyers can also pay a per-tonne residue-free supply fee. Ant-agent franchises would scale the model through local micro-entrepreneurs.
non_obvious_insight: Weaver ants were the world's first documented biocontrol, used in Chinese citrus groves for about 1,700 years. They never scaled because no one can patent or sell a colony, so there was no way to capture the value. The business is not the ant; it is the service wrapper, the verification data and the offtake contract that let someone get paid for a free natural crew.
first_30_days: Sign one cooperative in a cashew belt (Binh Phuoc in Vietnam or Mtwara in Tanzania). Recruit and train 20 farmers and 3 ant agents. Seed 500 trees in a pilot and compare pesticide spend and nut quality on matched control rows. Ask one processor to pre-commit to a residue-free premium.

title: Water Towers as Virtual Power Plants
one_liner: Aggregate municipal pump stations and elevated tanks into a controllable flexible load that dodges peak-coincident charges and earns demand-response and capacity payments, with a hard guarantee on pressure and fire reserve and an operator veto.
customer: Cities and districts that pump water, especially cities that own both the electric and water departments (common in the Midwest, Texas and the Southeast) and utilities with transmission-level or large demand-charge accounts. The buyer is the utilities director or the city manager, with the finance director as the champion.
problem: Electricity is one of the largest controllable costs for a pumped water system. Yet most pumping schedules are simple level setpoints written years ago, and operators keep tanks fat out of habit and fear. The unspoken rule is that nobody ever got fired for a full tank. Meanwhile the grid has turned pumping hours into money. Peak-coincident charges such as 4CP in ERCOT and peak load contribution tags in PJM are set by just a handful of hours per year. Capacity prices have spiked in recent auctions. Big load additions are pushing retail rates up. Water utilities are physically able to shift a large share of pumping, but no vendor is selling it to the 10-100k-population systems in a form an operator trusts.
solution: A small edge box or cloud service that reads tank levels, pump status and pressure from SCADA (OPC-UA or Modbus, read-only at first). It computes safe curtailment windows per station with hard constraints: fire and emergency reserve never touched, minimum pressure kept, projected demand over the event covered, water-age limits respected. It pre-cools tanks before predicted grid peaks and auto-releases if any constraint is threatened. Operators see one screen and can veto or end an event in one tap. Phase one is pure peak-coincident avoidance and time-of-use shifting, which needs no market enrollment. Phase two enrolls the stations as a curtailment resource through a demand-response aggregator partner or directly.
why_now: Recent PJM capacity auctions cleared at or near the price cap, on the order of $100k or more per curtailable megawatt per year before an aggregator's cut. Data center load growth is pushing capacity and transmission costs into retail rates, and RTOs and utilities are expanding demand-response programs. Edge controllers and OPC-UA gateways are cheap, and small teams can now build reliable forecasting for tank levels and peak intervals. (Auction figures are from memory. Verify current prices before pitching.)
revenue_model: 25-40% of verified savings and demand-response revenue, with no upfront cost to the utility and a small monthly platform fee. Utilities with both electric and water departments can be sold a bundled controls contract.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not physical but psychological and legal: operators are (rightly) terrified of a pressure or fire-flow failure. The winning product is not optimization software but a guarantee with a veto. Sell the operator the ability to stop it at any moment and the CFO the savings. Also, water and electric are often the same city, and the city has never put both budgets on one page.
first_30_days: Target three small cities that own both electric and water in ERCOT or PJM territory and have published tariffs. Get read-only SCADA access at one pump station, or historical CSV exports of tank levels and pump runs. Replay a year of the data to show what a 4CP or PLC avoidance schedule would have saved with reserves untouched. Bring that dollar figure to the city manager, and sign a shared-savings pilot on one pump station.

title: Work-Share Desk: Kurzarbeit for American Employers
one_liner: Administer state short-time compensation for mid-size employers so they can cut hours 20-40% instead of laying off skilled staff, with workers drawing pro-rated unemployment benefits.
customer: Employers with 50-800 employees (manufacturers, distributors, engineering firms, PEO-served businesses) in states with work-share programs, buying through the CFO, HR head or PEO.
problem: Roughly 33 states have short-time compensation programs, yet take-up is tiny because employers do not know they exist and the paperwork (plan applications, weekly certifications, state-specific rules, payroll integration) is painful. Layoffs then destroy trained staff who cost one to two times salary to replace when demand returns.
solution: A layoff-versus-work-share calculator for CFOs, plus a done-for-you service. It checks eligibility, prepares the state plan, connects payroll (Gusto, ADP, Rippling) to generate weekly certification data, provides employee communication scripts and tracks the effect on the employer's unemployment account. Expand state by state and through PEOs and manufacturers' associations.
why_now: The oil shock (crude above $100, diesel near $6) and the September 2026 Fed hike, the first since 2023, are cooling consumers. Unemployment is still low at about 4.1%, so executives want to keep hard-to-replace workers and are wary of repeating the 2022-2023 layoff-then-rehire cycle.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 setup fee plus $10-15 per participating employee per week, or 15% of verified savings versus layoff and rehire. PEO channel revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The program exists but nobody built the admin layer because the payoff only arrives in downturns. This is a business that sells the same product every recession and can build its state-rule database and PEO channel during the quiet years. Retention value is high precisely because the labor market is still tight.
first_30_days: Pick two manufacturing-heavy states with simple program rules (for example Ohio, Michigan or Pennsylvania). Publish a free layoff-versus-work-share calculator. Pitch 30 manufacturers via associations and PEOs and sign 5-10 at a $1,500 flat setup fee, doing the paperwork by hand at first.

title: Drug Safety Radar for Pet Medicines
one_liner: A real-world evidence network that reads clinic notes and insurance claims to spot adverse events for newly launched pet drugs and biologics, sold to manufacturers as pharmacovigilance.
customer: Animal-health manufacturers' safety and medical-affairs teams and biotechs launching first-in-class pet therapeutics; later regulators' contractors and insurers.
problem: Adverse-event reporting in vet medicine is voluntary and sparse, and clinics rarely file forms. New launches are arriving on conditional approvals and emergency authorizations, and the post-market evidence burden is growing.
solution: Consent-based feeds from ambient-scribe notes, PIMS and insurer claims. LLMs extract exposures and events, auto-draft FDA-format adverse-event reports in one click for clinics, and run signal detection with matched comparison cohorts. First product: a fixed-fee retrospective signal report for one drug class using one insurer's de-identified claims plus 20-50 clinics.
why_now: FDA has issued 15 emergency authorizations and 3 conditional approvals for screwworm drugs as of 2026-09-03, and Loyal's LOY-002 has cleared two of three technical sections with launch possible before year-end. Ambient scribes turn notes into structured text, and IDEXX/CoVet suggests data will get walled off by incumbents.
revenue_model: $50-250K per drug program per year, per-report fees, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: When launches lean on conditional approvals and emergency authorizations, evidence generation becomes a cost manufacturers must pay, not a nice-to-have. The winning data source is neutral: insurers plus clinics through scribes, not the PIMS vendors who will gate access.
first_30_days: Contact safety and medical-affairs leads at 5 mid-size animal-health companies. Propose a $40K retrospective signal study on a public safety question with an insurer data partner. Release a free one-click adverse-event drafting tool to 20 clinics to seed data.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.

title: Proof-of-Resident Public Comment
one_liner: Privacy-preserving verification that a public comment or 311 report comes from a real resident, without collecting their identity.
customer: City clerks, county boards, school districts, planning departments and state agencies running public-comment portals.
problem: Governments use GenAI to write documents, and vendors and activists use AI to flood the channels back. Councils and agencies can no longer tell 50 real residents from 5,000 bot-generated comments, so legitimate voices lose weight and hearings are contested.
solution: A comment widget that accepts a zero-knowledge proof from a mobile driver's license or wallet credential, proving residency and unique personhood without revealing name or address. Public dashboards show verified versus unverified counts, and the clerk keeps an audit log.
why_now: Mobile driver's licenses are live in a growing number of states, and wallet-level zero-knowledge proofs shipped in 2025. The signal-to-noise collapse from AI-generated submissions is now visible in procurement and public comment.
revenue_model: $5-30K per year per jurisdiction, with per-verification fees for state agencies and rulemaking dockets. Partner with agenda-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Verification without identity is the only approach that a hostile public will accept. Councils do not want a citizen database, they want a trustworthy count.
first_30_days: Build the widget with an open wallet-credential library in a state that supports mobile IDs. Pilot with one city clerk for a controversial hearing. Publish the verified-versus-unverified result.

title: ILIT Rescue After the Estate-Tax Cliff Disappeared
one_liner: A paid, documented review of irrevocable life insurance trusts built to pay estate tax that most families will never owe.
customer: Trustees (individuals and bank or trust companies), estate attorneys, and families holding ILITs with policies of $1M-$25M.
problem: For decades planners sold ILITs to fund federal estate tax. With the reported $15M-per-person exemption from 2026 (verify), many of these families will never owe it. Trusts keep paying premiums on policies that may be unnecessary, underfunded or poorly performing. Trustees fear fiduciary liability for doing nothing, yet nobody is paid to run the review.
solution: A 'trust-policy triage' service. Ingest the trust document and in-force illustration, classify the trust's purpose, and produce a decision memo: keep, reduce, 1035-exchange, sell, decant or terminate. It documents a prudent-process file for the trustee. Then execute through licensed partners (settlement broker, insurance agency, trust counsel).
why_now: The 2025 tax law reportedly raised and indexed the exclusion. About 10M life policies lapse per year (per the brief's cited market data), and the life-settlement market has active buyers (Coventry, Abacus). Wealth flows to heirs are large enough that leaving policy value on the table is now visible.
revenue_model: $2,500-$7,500 review fee per trust plus success fees on settled or exchanged policies where licensing allows.
non_obvious_insight: Fiduciary duty turns optimization into a mandatory review: trustees are exposed if they do nothing, so someone must be paid to produce the file even when the answer is 'keep'.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 estate attorneys and a licensed life-settlement broker. Pitch corporate trustees' special-assets desks. Run 10 reviews at a $1,500 intro price and learn which outcomes come up most.

title: Cell-Type-Restricted Promoters for Safer AAV
one_liner: AI-designed, primary-cell-validated regulatory sequences that switch AAV or LNP transgenes on only in target tissues and off in the liver.
customer: Gene therapy developers in muscle, heart and CNS (DMD, LGMD, cardiomyopathies) and capsid or CDMO companies wanting a detargeting cassette.
problem: High-dose systemic AAV caused acute liver failure deaths in 2025: three Sarepta patients, followed by a boxed warning and removal of non-ambulatory eligibility by Nov 14, 2025. Capsid engineering gets the attention, but the expression cassette is a second lever. Common promoters (CMV, CAG) are strong but non-specific, and miR-122 target sites only partly suppress liver expression.
solution: Generative design plus MPRA in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle cells and in primary human hepatocytes, ranking 10^4-10^5 sequences for high target and low liver expression. Deliver compact promoter-enhancer sets (under ~500 bp) with an optional miR-detargeting cassette, validated in vitro and in one partner rodent or NHP pilot.
why_now: The 2025 safety crisis is pushing dose reduction and liver detargeting. MPRA and generative sequence models are mature, DNA is cheap, and FDA's move toward human-relevant methods favors human primary-cell data.
revenue_model: $150-300k design-and-validation project plus a $50-200k license, with milestones or light royalties.
non_obvious_insight: The industry over-indexes on capsids, yet toxicity tracks where the transgene is expressed at dose. Compact regulatory parts are modular IP that stacks with any capsid, so one library serves many developers.
first_30_days: Run an MPRA on about 20k designed sequences in iPSC cardiomyocytes versus hepatocytes ($40-60k in reagents and sequencing). Publish a preprint and pitch 15 DMD, LGMD and cardiac programs on $50k pilots.

title: Dialysis Chair-Fill Rides Paid Per Completed Treatment
one_liner: A dedicated, route-based ride service for dialysis patients (same driver, same van loop, three times a week) priced per treatment completed instead of per trip, sold to the clinics and risk-bearing kidney-care companies that lose money on every missed session.
customer: Independent dialysis clinic groups and mid-sized operators worried about chair utilization, plus value-based kidney-care companies and Medicare Advantage ESRD plans that carry the hospitalization cost when a patient misses treatment.
problem: Medicaid non-emergency transport is a low-margin, hated business: pooled dispatch, late or missed pickups, and one-off rides for patients who actually have 156 predictable trips a year. The largest broker, ModivCare, went through Chapter 11 in 2025, so states and payers are unhappy with the incumbent. Meanwhile a missed dialysis session is expensive: in one study about 5% of patients were hospitalized within two days of a missed appointment versus 1.2% of those who attended. Medicare pays the clinic a bundled rate of about $282 per treatment in 2026, so every no-show is lost revenue, an idle chair and staff, and a sicker patient.
solution: Run dialysis like a bus route. Batch patients by chair shift and neighborhood, fix pickup windows, and assign dedicated driver-and-vehicle pairs so the patient sees the same person every time. Add SMS check-in, a same-day fallback ride through a taxi or rideshare partner, and a no-show guarantee. Report completed-treatment rates to the clinic weekly. Price by completed treatment (a round trip in the tens of dollars against roughly $280 of chair revenue), with an upside share for a lower missed-session rate. Structure it inside the Anti-Kickback local-transportation safe harbor, or bill risk-bearing plans and kidney-care companies directly, and confirm that with health-care counsel before launch.
why_now: ModivCare's bankruptcy and its emergence at the end of 2025 left NEMT contracts in flux and states re-examining brokers. CMS's kidney care models and Medicare Advantage special-needs plans are pushing risk onto companies that now feel every hospital day. Federal Medicaid cuts mean clinics and plans need cheaper ways to protect revenue rather than more benefits.
revenue_model: Fee per completed treatment (about $45-$75 round trip depending on wheelchair mix), with a bonus tied to reducing the clinic's missed-treatment rate. Second line: chemo and radiation patients on the same route logic.
non_obvious_insight: A dialysis chair is perishable inventory, like an airline seat, and the ride is a $50 cost that protects a $280 seat-day and a threefold hospitalization risk. NEMT is a terrible business because it treats a predictable, recurring, high-stakes patient as a random one-off trip. Treat those patients as a subscription route and the economics flip from a race to the bottom on price per mile to a premium on reliability.
first_30_days: Sell one independent operator with 3-5 clinics in one metro on a 60-day pilot covering 15-20 patients. Use two leased accessible vans, or subcontract a local NEMT operator, and two salaried drivers. Get the clinic's baseline missed-treatment rate from its own records and agree the target in writing before starting. Charge per completed treatment from day one, then take the data to a kidney-care company or MA plan for a larger contract.

title: Turn Podcast Fans Into Local Chapters
one_liner: A chapter-in-a-box that lets mid-size creators convert engaged, lonely audiences into weekly local meetups, with insurance, host training and venues handled.
customer: Superfans aged 18-34 paying about $12 a month for a local chapter. Creators with 50k-1M followers are the distribution partners on a revenue share. Brand sponsors pay for chapter access.
problem: Insiders treat parasocial attachment as a symptom of loneliness. But an audience with a shared in-group reference is already a pre-formed community, and creators' inboxes are full of 'is there a meetup in my city?' Creators cannot run 40 city chapters themselves because of liability, hosting, venues and safety. Discord and online-only communities do not fix in-person isolation.
solution: The platform reads audience data to find the top 10 fan-dense cities per creator. It recruits and trains volunteer hosts from top fans, provides liability insurance, a code of conduct and venue partnerships (breweries, cafes), and delivers a monthly 'creator drop' built for group listening or viewing. Each chapter runs weekly or biweekly with a 30-40 member target.
why_now: Fan-led IRL groups (run clubs, book clubs, hobby meetups) exploded through 2024-25. Feed fatigue and AI-slop backlash push young adults toward real-world belonging. Creators need revenue beyond volatile ad and sponsor income, and Meetup's post-acquisition policy troubles have left organizers looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: 20-25% of chapter dues, venue referral fees and sponsor packages. A 40-member chapter at $12 a month is $480 a month. Creators keep about 40% of dues.
non_obvious_insight: Parasocial is not the disease, it is the on-ramp. The cheapest cold start for local community is an audience that already shares references. What is missing is boring, outsourceable logistics and risk management.
first_30_days: Sign 3 niche-hobby creators with 100-300k audiences. Use their email or Patreon ZIP-code data to pick one city each. Recruit hosts from their Discords. Run the first brewery meetups and charge $12 a month from day one, aiming for 30 members per chapter.

title: Heat-Number Vault for Water-Project Compliance
one_liner: A registry that matches mill test reports to heat numbers for every pipe, valve and hydrant, producing audit-ready domestic-origin binders for SRF water projects and tariff-tier evidence for importers.
customer: Consulting engineers, contractors and waterworks distributors on state revolving fund (SRF) projects, at $1.5-4k per project. Foundries and importers claiming the 10% US-melt duty tier are the second buyer.
problem: SRF-funded water projects need domestic-origin documentation (American Iron and Steel, Build America Buy America). Section 232 duties now hinge on melt-and-pour or smelt-and-cast origin, and CBP is auditing origin. Certificates are PDFs that do not match heat numbers, and reviewers reject packages. Small engineering firms have no tooling.
solution: OCR and match mill test reports to heat numbers and purchase orders. Flag gaps before submittal, generate the compliance binder, and keep a verified-origin record that can be reused for customs and loan disbursement. Add manufacturer-side badges for foundries with clean records.
why_now: Full-customs-value 232 duties began Apr 2026, with 10% for US-melted metal. EPA announced $7.2B in FY2026 SRF funds, and USMCA rules of origin are tightening after the Jul 2026 non-renewal.
revenue_model: Per-project compliance fee ($1.5-4k), subscription for distributors, and a verification fee for foundries.
non_obvious_insight: Water utility procurement already forces the domestic-origin audit trail that tariff and reshoring tools lack, and the same data proves duty tiers. One dataset serves both the reshoring and water markets, and nobody has connected them.
first_30_days: Pitch five small-town engineering firms and two waterworks distributors. Do three projects by hand with a template plus OCR at $1.5k each. Use the misses and rejections to design the matching logic.

title: Work-From-Abroad Compliance Ledger for Employers
one_liner: A Slack-native ledger that tracks where remote employees actually work and flags tax, payroll, permanent-establishment and visa thresholds before 30 days from Lisbon becomes a liability.
customer: Remote-first companies with 50-1,000 employees, their HR and finance teams, and the tax advisors who serve them.
problem: Over 40 countries have nomad visas with thresholds from under USD 1,000 to over USD 7,000 per month, and some ban local employment. The EU Entry/Exit System has tracked non-EU travellers' 90/180-day stays automatically since April 2026. Employees informally work abroad, and companies do not know their exposure. Consumer trackers show individuals their days but give employers no aggregate view or approval flow.
solution: An opt-in ledger built from calendar entries, flight emails and optional device location, with a rules engine per country (183-day tests, 90/180 rules, permanent-establishment risk days, social-security thresholds, nomad-visa work rules). Employees request a workation, get an auto-check, then a manager approves. Export an evidence pack for tax advisors.
why_now: EES is fully live since April 2026, nomad visas keep multiplying, tax authorities are tightening, and return-to-office fights push employees to work from abroad informally.
revenue_model: USD 4-8 per employee per month with a USD 2K annual minimum, plus advisor referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the employer holding the liability, not the nomad. Information is free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so value has moved to compliance evidence and approval workflow.
first_30_days: Interview 20 HR leads at remote startups through remote-first communities. Build a Slack bot that answers '/workation Lisbon 6/1-6/30' with rules for 10 countries. Charge a flat USD 150 per month and partner with 2 international tax firms.

title: Worker-Owned Agentic Back-Office Cooperatives
one_liner: A franchise-in-a-box that helps laid-off finance and admin staff form co-ops running agent-leveraged bookkeeping, payroll and billing services for local small businesses, keeping the surplus themselves.
customer: Small businesses (5-50 employees) pay $600-2,500 a month. The co-ops pay a 5-8% platform fee, and are financed by cooperative-lending CDFIs, SBA microloans and workforce boards.
problem: The AI productivity dividend flows to platform owners while back-office workers lose jobs. Small businesses lack trusted human accountability (Bench's Dec 2024 shutdown stranded about 35k SMBs), and pure-AI bookkeepers still need a human on the hook.
solution: Co-op charter templates under state worker-co-op law, a shared agent stack (ledger automation, document intake, reconciliation) so each member handles 30-60 clients, a shared E&O policy, bank account and brand, client acquisition through local CPAs and chambers, and patronage dividends. Six-week onboarding.
why_now: Agentic accounting can now handle high-volume categorisation and reconciliation, finance-ops layoffs are rising, Bench's collapse left an opening, and co-op-friendly state laws and CDFI capital exist.
revenue_model: 5-8% of co-op revenue as a platform fee, tooling margin and $5-10k implementation fees per co-op.
non_obvious_insight: Ownership is the lever: workers who own the margin adopt agents fully, whereas employees hide productivity gains for fear of layoff. The scarce asset is trusted local human accountability, and agents supply the cost side.
first_30_days: Find 8-10 laid-off bookkeepers and controllers in one metro through layoff communities. Form a pilot co-op with a co-op legal clinic. Sign 15 SMB clients via three local CPAs and a chamber and run the first monthly closes.

title: Voice-Agent Cash-Price Negotiator for Imaging
one_liner: AI voice agents that call 20-30 local facilities, negotiate a guaranteed cash bundle for an MRI, CT or scope, and book it for the newly uninsured.
customer: Uninsured and high-deductible patients (Urban estimates 4.8M newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry; subsidy-cliff self-employed), small employers, and imaging centers, labs and ASCs with idle capacity.
problem: Posted prices are inconsistent and unusable, and cash prices for the same MRI can differ ~10x. Patients will not make 20 phone calls or negotiate, while facilities have idle slots.
solution: The patient submits an order. Agents call and email facilities for real quotes and slot availability, negotiate global-fee prepay bundles, filter for accreditation and quality, return one guaranteed price and book, with escrowed payment.
why_now: Real-time voice agents became reliable in 2025-26, and coverage loss is growing (ACA subsidies expired; Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027). Posted-price marketplaces exist but they don't negotiate dynamically.
revenue_model: $19-39 per booked procedure plus a 5-10% fee from facilities filling otherwise idle slots (cash-pay only, structured to avoid federal-program referral issues).
non_obvious_insight: Cash price is a negotiated market for empty slots. Discovery cost used to be too high per patient, and voice agents make it nearly free.
first_30_days: Concierge 50 MRI, CT and colonoscopy quotes in one metro with call scripts and an LLM voice agent on top. Publish the price spread, sign 5 imaging centers, and charge $29 per booking.
